titre: “Ecosystem,” a Word Coined Against an Idea
accroche: In 1935, at the request of the botanist Arthur Tansley, a colleague coins the word “ecosystem” against the idea of a forest-as-organism
contenu_vulgarise:
The word “ecosystem” is everywhere: digital ecosystem, business ecosystem, innovation ecosystem. We think it describes something obvious, the forest, the lake, the reef, with what lives in it.

It was not proposed to describe something obvious. It was proposed to settle a debate.

In 1935, the British botanist Arthur Tansley published in the journal Ecology a twenty-four-page article, “The use and abuse of vegetational concepts and terms” (Ecology, 16, pp. 284-307). In it he discusses the vocabulary of vegetation ecologists, and above all an idea then dominant, defended in the United States by Frederic Clements: a plant community supposedly develops like an organism, which is born, grows, reaches a final stage called the “climax,” and might even die.

## What He Rejects

Tansley does not flatly deny that the most fully developed communities show some features of organisms; he grants it, to a limited extent. What he refuses is to make a community an organism in the biological sense of the term, a being that would be born, reproduce and die as such. Pushing the analogy that far, for him, means sliding from the vocabulary of biology toward an almost vitalist one, in which the whole would acquire mysterious properties that no physical measurement can capture.

He proposes starting from somewhere else. What matters, he writes, is the whole system, in the sense of physics: not only the group of living beings, but also all the physical factors (soil, water, climate) with which it exchanges. Organisms and their environment form a single whole, linked by transfers of matter and energy.

The term chosen is “ecosystem.” According to historians of the discipline, Arthur Roy Clapham, a young colleague, suggested it at Tansley's request.

## A Tool, Not a Thing

The most striking thing is that Tansley does not claim ecosystems exist as objects with boundaries given by nature. He calls them “mental isolates”: cuts we make in the continuity of the world so that we can study it. A pond can be an ecosystem; the pond plus the meadow bordering it too; the whole Earth too.

This modesty is part of its strength. A historian of science, J. L. Dagg, argued in 2007 that the concept prevailed over its competitors precisely because it avoided vitalism and philosophical speculation, and kept to empirical foundations.

## The Shift

We think the concept was born of a discovery. It was born of a quarrel over vocabulary, and of a refusal: the refusal to let a metaphor pass for a complete explanation.

What we find in current usage, a well-delimited thing with sharp boundaries, is precisely what its author refused to see in it.

citation.texte: The more fundamental conception is, as it seems to me, the whole system (in the sense of physics), including not only the organism-complex, but also the whole complex of physical factors forming what we call the environment of the biome.
citation.source: The use and abuse of vegetational concepts and terms, Ecology 16 (3), 1935, pp. 284-307

carte.punch: “Ecosystem” was not born of a discovery. It was born of a refusal.
carte.idee: In 1935, at Tansley's request, the word is coined to rule out the idea of a forest as a full-fledged organism. He holds it to be a “mental isolate,” a cut made in order to study, not an object of nature.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: On the origin of the word and the role of Roy Clapham.

quiz.question: Why was the word “ecosystem” coined, at Tansley's request?
choix: To name the organism that a forest forms
To designate living things and the physical environment as a single system
To replace the word “biome,” which had become inaccurate
quiz.explication: He refused to make the community an organism in the full biological sense, even while conceding some organism-like traits to the most fully developed communities. The ecosystem brings living things and physical factors together into a system in the sense of physics, without vitalism. The other answers repeat the image he was qualifying or are foreign to his point.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Tansley mean by calling ecosystems “mental isolates”?
choix: Cuts made in order to study, not objects with sharp boundaries
That they exist only in the minds of ecologists, with no reality at all
That each ecosystem is isolated from the others by barriers
That only microscopic environments deserve the name
quiz_supplementaire.explication: An ecosystem is a convenient cut in the continuity of nature: a pond, a pond and its meadow, the whole Earth. It is neither unreal nor closed.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which idea was Tansley criticizing in the 1935 article?
choix: That a plant community is an organism
That plants compete with one another
quiz_supplementaire.explication: He was targeting Clements's conception, for whom the community developed as a quasi-organism up to a climax.
